Two proposals for the Foundation.

One asks for 0xPhilipp’s removal and a controlled transition. The other sets community governance rules and independent oversight for every director.

Each proposal stands independently. The revised transition requires all three directors to approve until a fourth joins, then three approvals. Proposal 2 can operate with the existing Board if Proposal 1 fails.

Two separate decisions

Support for governance reform does not require support for removing a particular director.

Proposal 1: removal and controlled transition

Withdraw confidence in 0xPhilipp and pursue lawful removal, preserve the fifth-director election, and elect a replacement separately. Verify operational continuity and complete the specified handover with independent checks.

All directors must approve until a fourth director is appointed, after which three approvals are required. That means 3-of-3, then 3-of-4 and 3-of-5. Recusal does not lower the minimum.

Read Proposal 1 and its exact amendment

Proposal 2: governance and independent accountability

Require implementation of passed community decisions within lawful authority, commission an independent financial and contract-authority review, and apply conflict and payment controls to all directors.

Maintain a public decision register, regular accountability reports and a community-approved framework for Board versus community decisions. This proposal removes no named director and grants no two-approval permission.

Read Proposal 2 and its exact amendments

Neither proposal can use the other’s unadopted powers to authorize itself. Passage, legal adoption and contract execution are separate events. The links above preserve the 16 November revision; the latest discussion texts may change.

Why we propose these changes

4855 approved a public election for a fifth director and community elections for future appointments. A296 was the Board resolution to implement it. Its two YES votes supplied 50/100 weight against a 75% threshold, so it expired and is recorded as rejected. There were no NO or ABSTAIN ballots. Either remaining director could have supplied the third YES; the record alone does not establish why either did not vote. At the 14 November evidence capture, 4855’s seven-day deadline to publish implementation owners had not expired. This historical capture does not establish a later missed deadline.

Our case for Proposal 2 is that failed ratification shows the need for a clear duty to implement passed Terra governance decisions. The proposed amendments would remove a second discretionary policy veto while preserving lawful-authority limits, non-waivable duties and case-specific execution judgment. A specific legal or technical obstacle would require disclosure, independent assessment and a lawful remedy, with unaffected work continuing.

Why remove 0xPhilipp?

The proposal argues for his removal based on the wider record: his stated position that ordinary community appointment votes are advisory, his support for A272’s removal and threshold change, beneficiary participation in payment approvals, and unresolved contract-control and milestone-acceptance questions. Those issues are documented below and in the full proposal. A296 adds an implementation failure involving two nonvoting directors; it does not establish that 0xPhilipp alone caused the failure or acted with a particular motive.

0xPhilipp argues that amendments and appointments require the Foundation’s governing procedures, eligibility checks and legal review. The proposed amendments retain those steps while removing a discretionary second veto over the community’s decision.

A272 failed while other Board business continued. The rejection of 4853 did not settle allegations against any director. The full proposal includes 0xPhilipp’s responses, A291’s proposed safeguards and his technical contributions. The payment and governance rules would apply to every director. This proposal seeks only 0xPhilipp’s removal.

How the transition is constrained

The 16 November revision removes the earlier temporary 2-of-3 permission. All three remaining directors must approve until a fourth is appointed. If the fifth-director election finishes before removal and four directors remain, three approvals are required. Proposal 1 preserves the ongoing election and does not delay it to create a three-director interval.

Discretionary interim authority ends after 60 calendar days from activation, or earlier when the fourth director joins. After day 60, limited caretaker acts still require all three directors. New related-party funding, increased director compensation and new long-term commitments are prohibited during the three-director interim configuration, subject only to separately authorized exceptions. If conflicts prevent approval, a lawful contingency or specific further authorization is needed; recusal cannot reduce the minimum.

What follows passage

Each proposal directs PD to acknowledge passage and name responsible implementers within seven calendar days, and publish an implementation dossier within 21 calendar days of passage. Both clocks start at passage. The dossier must identify governing documents, lawful adoption and enforcement routes, independent appointments, funding, contract control and dated completion plans. Missing items require a specific gap, responsible person, next action and completion date. Progress is reported weekly.

These are post-vote implementation duties. The texts do not require all supporting materials before submission, authorize unspecified expenditure or allow later documents to change the approved powers and safeguards. Additional funding and material changes need the applicable further approvals.

Handover must be demonstrated

Both proposals preserve the original TLA commitments to transfer administration after one month and ownership permissions after three months. They credit completed transfers and require a current contract-by-contract schedule, including TLA global configuration and Foundation-used Treasury and v3 contracts, with direct and indirect control paths.

Source, build, licence and maintenance-access records, independent operating-readiness checks and a costed contingency plan belong in the 21-day dossier. A transfer of one role does not prove all upstream control transferred; a missing public repository does not establish what access or rights exist. The proposals do not confer ownership of unrelated ERIS infrastructure or authorize an automatic withdrawal or shutdown.

Review the accountability deadlines and adoption safeguards. Removal is a confidence decision; it does not establish wrongdoing. Independent review must consider all relevant directors, preserve responses and distinguish missing evidence from established failures.

4855, in plain language

Four directors can split two against two. A fifth gives the board another equal voice to reach a decision.

The community would choose the new director. Volunteers would have 14 days to put themselves forward, followed by seven days for public questions. Each candidate would then face a separate Terra governance vote. Voters could support more than one candidate.

Three directors would have to agree. The intended result is five equal seats and at least three affirmative approvals for multisig decisions. The fifth director would have one vote, the same as everyone else. Existing directors would remain in office.

The Foundation’s Treasury would fund the candidate-ballot deposits. The selected candidate would have to complete identity and eligibility checks before joining. The proposal also asks for a bylaw change so future directors are chosen through community elections.

Passage approved this process; it did not elect a candidate. The Foundation still has to complete the appointment, change the multisig and adopt the bylaw amendment through its governing procedures. The chain vote does not execute those changes automatically.

Why the ampLUNA voting bloc matters

A small group of participants can decide how a much larger pool of LUNA votes on who oversees the Foundation.

The ampLUNA analysis below preserves the 05 November 2026, 14:56 UTC snapshot and separately dated lock queries. Its voting figures and contract permissions describe those captures. 4855 has since passed. At the voting snapshot, YES was 68.51% excluding abstentions, VETO was 31.04% of all votes, and participation was 39.97%. Historical tally.

ampLUNA uses an internal vote before casting the hub’s Terra ballot. Users who lock ampLUNA receive internal voting power, called vAMP. Once participants supply at least 10% of that power, their voting split directs the hub’s whole ballot.

For 4855, two addresses supplied 11.38% of the internal voting power. Both chose NO WITH VETO, so the hub cast its entire ballot that way. The other internal voting power does not automatically count as abstaining. This does not show that all ampLUNA holders chose or supported that position.

One voter is the publicly linked wallet of 0xPhilipp, a current PF director; the other is the ERIS protocol-fee recipient. The concern is the extent to which this small participation can shape a vote about the Foundation’s own governance. A director has a direct interest in that subject, and the two addresses do not establish two independent decision-makers.

The hub’s direct ballot overrides its validators’ votes for the hub’s delegations. That gives these internal votes influence beyond their own locked holdings. These facts warrant scrutiny of representation and independence; they do not establish improper conduct or determine the final result of 4855.

How much did the two wallets lock?

Two wallets locked the equivalent of about 33,750 LUNA. Their votes set the ballot on proposal 4855 for the hub, which had about 32.85 million LUNA delegated at the snapshot.

The ERIS fee wallet locked 7,864.405222 ampLUNA, worth about 19,190.92 LUNA at the captured rate. Its lock expires on 30 October 2028. The ERIS validator wallet locked 5,966.337711 ampLUNA, worth about 14,559.21 LUNA. Its lock expires on 06 December 2027. Both unlock dates start at 00:00 UTC.

On 3 November, two days before voting opened, the fee wallet extended its lock by 47 weeks and deposited no additional ampLUNA in that transaction. Holding the other votes and locks fixed, the two wallets would have supplied 8.43% of eligible voting power without the extension. With it they supplied 11.38%, clearing the 10% quorum.

The voting keys directed the hub ballot on 4855. They gave the voters no permission to withdraw or spend the pool’s LUNA. The fee wallet’s escrow history starts at 1,000 ampLUNA in February 2023 and records later increases. The source of the deposited tokens remains unverified.

The LUNA equivalents use the hub exchange rate captured on 05 November 2026, 20:52 UTC. The pool size comes from the earlier ballot snapshot above.

How escrow votes become a chain vote

Holding ampLUNA alone does not create a separate Terra ballot for the LUNA backing it. The staking hub holds those delegations.

  1. Lock and vote

    Users lock ampLUNA in the voting escrow. Their voting power includes a fixed component and a time-dependent component, calculated for the proposal’s end period. They choose YES, NO, ABSTAIN or NO WITH VETO.

  2. Reach the 10% quorum

    The proposal gauge is currently configured for a 10% quorum of escrow voting power. At this snapshot, two addresses supplied 11.38%, both voting NO WITH VETO.

  3. Apply the participating split

    The gauge passes the participants’ weighted split to the hub. All recorded participation was NO WITH VETO, so the hub cast 100% NO WITH VETO for its delegated stake.

The quorum is a percentage of escrow voting power, not all ampLUNA holders or all LUNA delegated by the hub. Nonparticipants do not automatically receive an ABSTAIN share. For example, a qualifying 60/40 YES/NO split would instruct a 60/40 hub vote, subject to rounding.

A direct hub ballot overrides the underlying validators’ votes for the hub’s delegations. Other delegators retain their own voting rights. The reported 32.85M LUNA is a contemporaneous delegation measure, not a fixed final vote weight.

Who can change the voting rules?

The hub’s internal owner and its migration administrator hold different powers.

ERIS configuration owner

The live hub and proposal gauge name terra1kefa…klgzl as owner. This is a normal single-key chain account, not the PF multisig. That describes on-chain authorization, not how many people can access its key.

The hub owner can replace the authorized voting operator. Under the current code, the replacement operator can cast a normal or weighted hub vote without passing the escrow gauge’s quorum. The owner cannot directly vote while a different operator remains configured, but can change that configuration first.

The proposal-gauge owner can register proposals, choose their stored end time, change the quorum, switch between weighted and single-option voting, remove a user’s recorded votes from active proposals, and delete proposal records. Removing a vote record does not permanently bar that user from voting again.

Phoenix Foundation migration administrator

The hub’s migration admin is the PF DAO. Through its own approval process, it can authorize replacement hub code. The hub is now code 2726, version 1.8.0. Migration authority is broader than a permission to change today’s settings; replacement code could change the rules themselves. It does not make PF the current internal owner.

The voting gauge and escrow retain a separate migration admin, terra1q0vny…q5tew. The escrow also permits its owner or guardian to blacklist addresses and remove their voting power. These permissions are capabilities, not evidence that they were used to produce the captured 4855 vote.

Other hub powers and verification limits

The hub owner can change validator eligibility and delegation strategy, tune and rebalance delegations, change the fee recipient and reward fee within the current 10% cap (currently 8%), and adjust batch and expected-unbonding periods. The live periods are three days and 21 days. The v1.8.0 source rejects zero timing values but provides no operational upper bound beyond the integer type; changing these settings does not change Terra’s staking-module unbonding period.

The live hub, gauge and escrow bytecode hashes match their published release binaries. The associated release source was inspected; an independent reproducible build and complete security audit were not performed. In weighted mode, falling below quorum emits no replacement ballot, so an earlier chain ballot can remain. Deleting a gauge record does not itself retract that ballot.

4853 and 4855 both ask governance to change PF’s governance

The shared mechanism is a Terra governance mandate followed by implementation through the Foundation’s governing procedures. The proposed changes differ.

The published bylaws contain limits and tensions discussed in the historical review.No executable messages. It did not automatically remove a director or change the multisig threshold.
4855 · passed 12 NovemberPublic nomination and election of a fifth equal director, at least three affirmative multisig approvals out of five, and specific amendments requiring community elections for future appointments.No executable messages. Appointment requires eligibility/KYC and an authorized multisig change. Bylaw amendments require adoption under §7.3.

4853’s submission shows that a chain vote was already being used to seek changes to PF’s governance. Its rejection does not establish that its allegations were true or create an adopted legal precedent. 4855 uses an ordinary appointment route and does not declare an emergency or seek removal powers.

The governance issue is concrete: the community voted on who should participate in PF decisions, while the ampLUNA mechanism lets a qualifying group of escrow voters direct pooled LUNA in that same vote. Readers should be able to see the participating interests, the quorum and the owner powers when assessing how representative that vote is.

Four concerns in the records

0xPhilipp helped approve releases from ERIS’s Creda grant

0xPhilipp proposed and voted YES on A209, enabling 200,000 USDC for Creda’s first three milestones. Vini and MB supplied the other two YES votes. A215 later enabled another 10,000 USDC for analytics, bringing the grant total to 210,000 USDC.

Both were three-director approvals. The Treasury action marks all four milestones claimed. These amounts funded the project; they do not establish personal profit or independent acceptance of the work.

Creda’s grant, approval votes and milestones

The handover left some contract powers unchanged

ERIS proposal 9 gave the Phoenix board upgrade control over two contracts. The hub’s internal owner and the ICS20 contract’s internal governance setting did not change. Other Treasury and TLA permissions also remain.

A contract’s upgrade administrator and its internal owner can have different powers. The records identify authorized addresses; they do not establish who holds every key.

Which powers transferred and which remain

Payment records do not show acceptance of every milestone

Phoenix grants identified for Creda, Votion and the migration app total 265,000 USDC. Transfers and claimed milestones are recorded; independent acceptance of every deliverable has not been established.

AADAO separately reports Votion’s Hydro work complete and jointly verified. Project funding is not personal profit, and a later unfinished page does not prove that no work occurred.

Funding, delivered work and missing acceptance records

A272 proposed concentrating board approval power

A272 proposed removing Vini and lowering the approval threshold to 60%, allowing two of the remaining three seats to approve an action. It failed: 0xPhilipp and MB voted YES, Rose voted NO and Vini was absent.

The board remained four seats with a 75% threshold. 4853 later sought a supervisor and removal-facilitation powers over the same dispute, but was rejected. A later removal and threshold change could reopen the concentration risk; neither happens automatically on passage.

The route from failed A272 to proposal 4853

Historical 4853 voting scenario

In the 30 October 2026, 16:31 UTC snapshot, switching the ampLUNA hub to a full YES vote would raise YES from 24.81% to 41.00% of non-abstain votes, still below the required majority if nothing else changed.

The hub has a native ABSTAIN ballot, and its vAMP gauge records abstention voting power. The calculation models a change to that ballot; it does not establish a voting agreement.

Questions for continuing oversight

  1. Disclose financial interests

    Directors, Think Tank members, validators and contractors should disclose relevant payments, grants, hosting arrangements and voting interests under their public role or handle.

    Who has which role

  2. Publish voting instructions

    Explain planned hub and gauge votes. Where a validator follows a DAO mandate, finish the internal vote first. Lion DAO’s validator changed to YES while its A33 vote was still open.

    Lion DAO’s voting sequence

  3. Provide the missing approval records

    Publish recusal decisions, milestone acceptance, contract handover terms and any approved extensions. Retain the ballots, payment records and responses for independent review.

    Proposed governance changes

Who controls the community’s assets?

The control review focuses on TLA and Treasury: infrastructure funded to manage chain liquidity and community funds. TLA’s promised handover remains incomplete, and Treasury retains an ERIS upgrade administrator. Creda, Votion and Estima are treated separately as application-development grants.
